DURBAN's DRUG TURF WAR

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A drug lord gunned down in his home. His assailants shot and beheaded out in the open in broad daylight as a turbulent gangsters’ turf war comes to a head in Durban.

Unique Selling Point:
- FOOTAGE OF EXTREME MOB JUSTICE
- AL COPONE TYPE DRUG LORD FIGURE - interesting dynamics
- STORY NOT WELL KNOWN NATIONALLY

Summary:
Nortorius Drug Lord Teddy Mafia was loved and loathed by the Chatsworth community. His legacy came to a gruesome end when the gunmen that shot him, were hacked and set alight in full view of the community while police stood at a distance, calling for backup as they too feared the wrath of the mob.

This savageness is the result of mob justice colliding with gangsterism. We delve into the driving forces and unpack the disturbing reality of life in Chatsworth – a community crippled by poverty and drug addiction.

Further information:
A RUN DOWN OF THE EVENTS
Yaganathan Pillay, 62, commonly known as Teddy Mafia, at about 2pm Teddy Mafia told his daughter he was expecting visitors. They were let in and taken to meet with Teddy. The daughter heard gun shots and ran to check what happened. Teddy had been shot. Was it a hit or an accident – is yet to be established.

The community apparently apprehended both suspects when they tried to leave the scene. Outraged at the death of Pillay, several people chopped the heads off the two men. The bodies were left outside Pillay’s home at the intersection of Table Mountain and Taurus Street. Rubble, tree branches and planks were placed on them and they were set alight. When police attempted to extinguish the fire bricks and stones were aimed at them.

According to SAPS, when police officers arrived the community opened fire on them. Police called in the Public Order Policing Unit who dispersed the crowd with no injuries. It wan’t the first time residents in the area had attacked police officers. In January 2019 it was reported that about 200 residents had turned on officers conducting a drug raid in Shallcross, in the same street where Teddy lived.

Teddy Mafia succumbed to his injuries in a Chatsworth hospital.

THE LOVE / HATE RELATIONSHIP
Pillay was loved and despised by the Chatsworth community. The Shallcross community, which benefited from his charity including food parcels. Word in the community is that he put kids through school and university and even helped people pay their utility bills.
It’s said that if you were in trouble you could turn to Teddy who would help where he could. Alleged criminal syndicates and leaders are often viewed as Robin Hood-type characters as the proceeds of crime often go back into the community, so if a drug lord is killed, it would directly affect the community. It’s a tactic utilised by criminal syndicates around the world who purposely and strategically look after their community so they are given cover and protection when the time comes.
The reality is whether it is an act of vigilantism because of mistrust in police, a message by associates of Teddy Mafia or the community seeking revenge because of who was killed, there was a total sense of impunity and disregard for the law.
At least two people a day die as a result of vigilante or group attacks in South Africa, according to the Institute for Security Studies. Violence is so normalised in society that ‘ordinary’ people commit horrific acts.

UNSOLVED DRIVEBY SHOOTINGS THE START OF VIOLENT CLASHES
And in March 2020 Pillay’s son Devendren was fatally wounded in a drive-by shooting in Shallcross (Chatsworth).

It is understood that Devendren Lionel Pillay, 32, and Claudene Rampersad, 32, had been standing in the driveway of Rampersad’s home on Alpine Drive, Shallcross, when a white Toyota Corolla, with a number of occupants, drove past and fired multiple shots — killing the pair. Around the same time there were at three other relatives of Teddy taken out, and what was believed to be retaliation shooting killing some of his rival gang members.

TEDDY’s BRUSHES WITH THE LAW
Despite Teddy Mafia’s reign spanning more than three decades – he was never convicted of drug offences. He has been arrested a few times – the most recent was arrested in April 2020 during a raid at his home, where police allegedly found unlicensed firearms, R700,000 in cash, and gold and silver coins with an estimated value of R250,000. Charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition, he was released on R5,000 bail at the Chatsworth magistrate’s court and ordered to appear at the local police station twice a week.

Previous convictions dating back to the 1970s for dealing in alcohol, driving without a licence and possession of an unlicensed firearm. But no drug convictions.

TEDDY’s BROTHER SPEAKS OUT
Ronnie Pillay, lambasted the police, saying there was a drug war taking place in Shallcross and police had done nothing to make any arrests in relation to the eight murders which had occurred since December 2019.

“There is corruption with police and criminals. The police are well aware of what is transpiring in this country — they are well aware. There is a drug war taking place here, there's a drug war in regard to sales and distribution.”
He went on to claim there were links between certain “drug lords” in Durban and senior police officials, claiming the rot stretched as far as senior officials in Pretoria


WHAT WE HAVE
- Videos from the scene – the beheadings, the burning of the bodies
- Voice Notes from the police on the scene calling for back up.
- Teddy Mafia’s brother on camera.

INTERVIEWS
- SAPS
- RONNIE PILLAY – BROTHER: CRITICISED SAPS FOR SITUATION IN COMMUNITY – DOESN’T DENY BROTHER’S ILLEGAL ACTIVITIES – SAYS HE WAS WHO HE WAS.
- ORRIN SINGH – JOURNALIST: ABOUT THE BACKGROUND AND HOW EVENTS UNFOLDED ON THE DAY
- ANDREW FAULL – ISS: THE SAVAGE COMBINATION OF GANGSTERISM AND MOB JUSTICE.
- COP INSIDER – STILL WORKING ON IT – WITHIN SAPS COPS FEEL THEY ARE TO BLAME – THE ORGANISED CRIME INVESTIGATIONS ARE INEFFECTIVE BECAUSE COPS ARE ON THE TAKE AND DESPITE BEING LAW ENFORCERS THEY FEAR THE GANGS.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO Drugs, guns and murder, are a way of life for gangsters who feud over turf to maximize illicit profits.

LINK: These criminal syndicates don’t operate in isolation – territories overlap and worlds collide in the fight to control illegal networks – and with big money to be made – these clashes are moving out of the shadows.

VO: The spotlight was cast on the Underworld in Durban early in January. An alleged drug lord, Yaganathan Pillay known as Teddy Mafia, was gunned down in his home in Shallcross.

It’s an area crippled by social struggles from poverty to extreme drug addiction.

Both loved and loathed - Teddy Mafia was well-known in his community and in police circles explains this cop who spoke to us on condition of anonymity.

INSIDER: Teddy Mafia is a drug lord, he portrayed himself as Robin hood. Where he would feed and take care of the underprivileged, but sell drugs to the same people's children.

VO: Just moments after Teddy’s shooting, the two alleged gunmen were shot and killed.

The scene that erupted outside the house was nothing short of barbaric. The imagery in this clip is too graphic to broadcast.

Behind the blur, the bodies of the two alleged shooters believed to be responsible for Teddy Mafia’s death, lay in the middle of the road. There is a man wielding an axe. He is busy chopping off the gunmen’s heads.

UPSOUND CHOP, CHOP.

VO: That is the sound of the axe decapitating the bodies. It stops when one of the heads is severed.

DR LAMB: You don't go from doing no violence to chopping or cutting off someone's head.

VO: Incidents of this level of hyper-violence occur where violence has become normalised explains Criminologist Dr Guy Lamb.

DR LAMB: An average person wouldn't be able to do this because of a conscience. But in the case of someone who is a psychopath or a sociopath, a psychopath, whether it's the sense of around , you feel no emotion in doing this.

VO: This scene played out in full view of the community while police stood at a distance, calling for back-up, as they too feared the mob.

CALLS FROM COPS
– SIREN – MEMBER REQUIRE BACK UP.
taking someone’s head off – community very volatile here.

INSIDER The community showed no regard to the police. They see two people have been murdered. The police have a responsibility to act, but because the community know so much about them, they stood back and allowed it to take place.

VO: The mob then proceeded to set the bodies alight in the middle of the street as a final message.

CALLS FROM COPS
Please man, we need back up here, urgently – please man// both head decapitated- one set a light, other one about to set alight here

MASA: Is this what we can expect when mob justice collides with gangsterism.
DR LAMB: Absolutely. I mean, we've seen this happen playing out and certainly in Western Cape // where we're seeing individuals who are linked to providing sort of certain welfare to certain members of the community and then they're assassinated, it has these these are kind of very violent consequences.

VO: Ronnie Pillay is Teddy Mafia’s brother. While the details around the shooting are sketchy, he says Teddy was expecting the men and met with them privately at the house.

RONNIE: all of a sudden, you have shot two shots fired // when they came down they saw Teddy had two bullets - one in his hand and one in his forehead. Immediately these guys // started blaming each other. First, they say they don't know who did it and then they started blaming each other.

VO: The only three men that know what really happened, are all dead. Journalist Orrin Singh has been covering the story extensively.

MASA: Was it a hit or an accident?
ORRIN: Right now we can’t be sure, it would be an educated guess or speculation.// Rumours have been rife within the community//

VO: But not having facts didn’t stop the community from taking the law into their own hands that day.

LINK: When it comes to committing crime you’d think there’s a general fear of being caught, a fear for law enforcement. But instead the balance has shifted where the cops now fear communities who act with complete impunity and disregard for the law.

VO: Pillay believes the community reaction was a long time coming.

RONNIE: This was boiling in the community and somehow it’s going to be let off. And I didn't expect it to be let out in such a drastic manner. But this was culminating to that where you saw the beheading and the killing, people were fed up.

VO: The act of vigilantism is fuelled by a need for instant justice explains Dr Lamb.

DR LAMB: It’s More of a lack of faith or loss of faith within the criminal justice system as the sense that the individuals who perpetrated this crime will not be brought to book, // the role of the police in all of this is the sense that the police aren't going to do anything. // this is where we have to take care of managing the situation ourselves and enforcing our own law.

VO: This lawlessness in the Shallcross and Chatsworth area has been building up since 2019. 7 people had been taken out in 6 separate drive-by shooting incidents confirmed Singh.

ORRIN: at least four of these murders were relatives of teddy mafia’s, including his son, who was killed in March last year in a drive by shooting. And from what we understand, after his son's murder, Teddy Mafia was never the same.

VO: To date no arrests have been made.

RONNIE: these gangsters are walking the doing this things, this murder in a drive by shooting it with impunity because knowing that it would be caught. // Nobody, no investigation. Nobody has been caught. Nothing has transpired. INT1M7

ORRIN: the sentiment on the ground is it's just sort of resentment and anger towards the police,// And I think that sort of all spilled over. And that's why we saw what happened on Teddy Mafia Street on the day of his murder. INT2M11

RONNIE Iit was heading in that direction. I'm not justifying the beheading and chopping and killing, but from the inadequacy of the police force to addressing the key issue.INT1M14

VO: Pillay is convinced that the 7 murders in just 13 months are linked to a fight for drug turf.

RONNIE: this is a drug war that is taking place. If you take over this area for drugs, you take out the opposition, you can do anything you want to do?
MASA: What do you say to people who say your brother was at the centre of this and he too was a druglord?
RONNIE: Neither will i acknowledge or deny - never in any time has my brother been charged or prosecuted for a drug offence - my brother was a very gifted person, a very gifted person when it comes to businesses

VO: But according to the police insider these businesses included illegal operations.

INSIDER: It was common knowledge that he sold drugs. They are obviously going to make him seem like a saint. Yes, he did feed the community. He did do that. But that's a way of him winning the community over.

VO: It’s a tactic utilised by criminal syndicates around the world - they strategically look after their community so they are given cover and protection when the time comes.

DR LAMB: Teddy Mafia seems to be quite an important community figure, not only involved in crime, but in the sense of the proceeds of crime, did flow to certain community members who are seen as a key benefactor in these particular areas

VO: Even Police Minister Bheki Cele questioned why a known gangster and drug dealer was still out there.

Teddy Mafia operated for more than three decades – despite being arrested a few times, his record shows he was never convicted of drug offences.

ORRIN: the cases that he was arrested and charged for relate to possession of illegal illegal firearms, ammunition, attempted murder, resisting arrest and dealing in drugs and being in possession of drugs. INT1M5

VO: A number of these cases were withdrawn, explained the police insider.

MASA: why he was never convicted
INSIDER: Due to corruption. Due to certain members of the police protecting him. And either warn him of planned operations, or purposely not conduct the operation properly where maybe a search warrant won’t be obtained.
MASA: So how come this was allowed to happen and continue for this long?
INSIDER: Some cops on the payroll are not all, some are.

VO: The KZN Provincial Police did not grant us an interview, nor did they reply to our questions in writing.

Whether Teddy Mafia was more Robin Hood or more druglord is irrelevant - the rule of law must prevail. Pillay believes his community has been let down.

RONNIE: Many a time, not once, many a time, so when we pick up the phone and reports the // police stations, there was no response. It was as if, you know what, let them kill themselves. and we are not concerned about that//INT1M4//

VO: Pillay is adamant that the gruesome scenes that played out after his brother’s shooting, was a culmination of the community’s frustration.

RONNIE: This was the anger that was brewing in the community for quite some time because of the inability of the police themselves to carrying out the task, not responding. INT1M9

VO: But until the criminal justice system has proven it effectiveness to South Africans, mob justice will continue to be meted out believes Dr Lamb.

DR LAMB: We will continue to see cases happening where communities feel // Criminals must be punished and there must be the punishment must be visible to members of the community to demonstrate to others that you shouldn't do this. // That will continue to happen certainly in SA vigilante violence is not going away.


 
PROMO 1
VO: When mob justice collides with gangsterism - the violence is next level. An alleged Durban drug lord is killed. The two suspected gunmen, are shot, beheaded and burnt on the streets for all to see.

PROMO 2
VO: We investigate how the killing of alleged Durban drug lord led to violence when his killers were beheaded and set alight in broad daylight on the streets of community crippled by drug addiction.

PROMO 3
VO: Heads chopped off in broad daylight and bodies set alight – is this what happens when gangsterism and mob justice collide? We explore these dynamics behind a drug turf war in Durban.

CALLS FROM COPS Please man, we need back up here, urgently – please man// both head decapitated- one set a light, other one about to set alight here MASA: Is this what we can expect when mob justice collides with gangsterism. DR LAMB: Absolutely. I mean, we've seen this happen playing out and certainly in Western Cape // where we're seeing individuals who are linked to providing sort of certain welfare to certain members of the community and then they're assassinated, it has these these are kind of very violent consequences. VO: Ronnie Pillay is Teddy Mafia’s brother. While the details around the shooting are sketchy, he says Teddy was expecting the men and met with them privately at the house. RONNIE: all of a sudden, you have shot two shots fired // when they came down they saw Teddy had two bullets - one in his hand and one in his forehead. Immediately these guys // started blaming each other. First, they say they don't know who did it and then they started blaming each other. VO: The only three men that know what really happened, are all dead. Journalist Orrin Singh has been covering the story extensively. MASA: Was it a hit or an accident? ORRIN: Right now we can’t be sure, it would be an educated guess or speculation.// Rumours have been rife within the community// VO: But not having facts didn’t stop the community from taking the law into their own hands that day. LINK: When it comes to committing crime you’d think there’s a general fear of being caught, a fear for law enforcement. But instead the balance has shifted where the cops now fear communities who act with complete impunity and disregard for the law. VO: Pillay believes the community reaction was a long time coming. RONNIE: This was boiling in the community and somehow it’s going to be let off. And I didn't expect it to be let out in such a drastic manner. But this was culminating to that where you saw the beheading and the killing, people were fed up. VO: The act of vigilantism is fuelled by a need for instant justice explains Dr Lamb. DR LAMB: It’s More of a lack of faith or loss of faith within the criminal justice system as the sense that the individuals who perpetrated this crime will not be brought to book, // the role of the police in all of this is the sense that the police aren't going to do anything. // this is where we have to take care of managing the situation ourselves and enforcing our own law. VO: This lawlessness in the Shallcross and Chatsworth area has been building up since 2019. 7 people had been taken out in 6 separate drive-by shooting incidents confirmed Singh. ORRIN: at least four of these murders were relatives of teddy mafia’s, including his son, who was killed in March last year in a drive by shooting. And from what we understand, after his son's murder, Teddy Mafia was never the same. VO: To date no arrests have been made. RONNIE: these gangsters are walking the doing this things, this murder in a drive by shooting it with impunity because knowing that it would be caught. // Nobody, no investigation. Nobody has been caught. Nothing has transpired. INT1M7 ORRIN: the sentiment on the ground is it's just sort of resentment and anger towards the police,// And I think that sort of all spilled over. And that's why we saw what happened on Teddy Mafia Street on the day of his murder. INT2M11 RONNIE Iit was heading in that direction. I'm not justifying the beheading and chopping and killing, but from the inadequacy of the police force to addressing the key issue.INT1M14 VO: Pillay is convinced that the 7 murders in just 13 months are linked to a fight for drug turf. RONNIE: this is a drug war that is taking place. If you take over this area for drugs, you take out the opposition, you can do anything you want to do? MASA: What do you say to people who say your brother was at the centre of this and he too was a druglord? RONNIE: Neither will i acknowledge or deny - never in any time has my brother been charged or prosecuted for a drug offence - my brother was a very gifted person, a very gifted person when it comes to businesses VO: But according to the police insider these businesses included illegal operations. INSIDER: It was common knowledge that he sold drugs. They are obviously going to make him seem like a saint. Yes, he did feed the community. He did do that. But that's a way of him winning the community over. VO: It’s a tactic utilised by criminal syndicates around the world - they strategically look after their community so they are given cover and protection when the time comes. DR LAMB: Teddy Mafia seems to be quite an important community figure, not only involved in crime, but in the sense of the proceeds of crime, did flow to certain community members who are seen as a key benefactor in these particular areas VO: Even Police Minister Bheki Cele questioned why a known gangster and drug dealer was still out there. Teddy Mafia operated for more than three decades – despite being arrested a few times, his record shows he was never convicted of drug offences. ORRIN: the cases that he was arrested and charged for relate to possession of illegal illegal firearms, ammunition, attempted murder, resisting arrest and dealing in drugs and being in possession of drugs. INT1M5 VO: A number of these cases were withdrawn, explained the police insider. MASA: why he was never convicted INSIDER: Due to corruption. Due to certain members of the police protecting him. And either warn him of planned operations, or purposely not conduct the operation properly where maybe a search warrant won’t be obtained. MASA: So how come this was allowed to happen and continue for this long? INSIDER: Some cops on the payroll are not all, some are. VO: The KZN Provincial Police did not grant us an interview, nor did they reply to our questions in writing. Whether Teddy Mafia was more Robin Hood or more druglord is irrelevant - the rule of law must prevail. Pillay believes his community has been let down. RONNIE: Many a time, not once, many a time, so when we pick up the phone and reports the // police stations, there was no response. It was as if, you know what, let them kill themselves. and we are not concerned about that//INT1M4// VO: Pillay is adamant that the gruesome scenes that played out after his brother’s shooting, was a culmination of the community’s frustration. RONNIE: This was the anger that was brewing in the community for quite some time because of the inability of the police themselves to carrying out the task, not responding. INT1M9 VO: But until the criminal justice system has proven it effectiveness to South Africans, mob justice will continue to be meted out believes Dr Lamb. DR LAMB: We will continue to see cases happening where communities feel // Criminals must be punished and there must be the punishment must be visible to members of the community to demonstrate to others that you shouldn't do this. // That will continue to happen certainly in SA vigilante violence is not going away. PROMO 1 VO: When mob justice collides with gangsterism - the violence is next level. An alleged Durban drug lord is killed. The two suspected gunmen, are shot, beheaded and burnt on the streets for all to see. PROMO 2 VO: We investigate how the killing of alleged Durban drug lord led to violence when his killers were beheaded and set alight in broad daylight on the streets of community crippled by drug addiction. PROMO 3 VO: Heads chopped off in broad daylight and bodies set alight – is this what happens when gangsterism and mob justice collide? We explore these dynamics behind a drug turf war in Durban.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A drug lord gunned down in his home. His assailants shot and beheaded out in the open in broad daylight as a turbulent gangsters’ turf war comes to a head in Durban.

metadata.Summary: Nortorius Drug Lord Teddy Mafia was loved and loathed by the Chatsworth community. His legacy came to a gruesome end when the gunmen that shot him, were hacked and set alight in full view of the community while police stood at a distance, calling for backup as they too feared the wrath of the mob. This savageness is the result of mob justice colliding with gangsterism. We delve into the driving forces and unpack the disturbing reality of life in Chatsworth – a community crippled by poverty and drug addiction.
metadata.Further information: A RUN DOWN OF THE EVENTS Yaganathan Pillay, 62, commonly known as Teddy Mafia, at about 2pm Teddy Mafia told his daughter he was expecting visitors. They were let in and taken to meet with Teddy. The daughter heard gun shots and ran to check what happened. Teddy had been shot. Was it a hit or an accident – is yet to be established. The community apparently apprehended both suspects when they tried to leave the scene. Outraged at the death of Pillay, several people chopped the heads off the two men. The bodies were left outside Pillay’s home at the intersection of Table Mountain and Taurus Street. Rubble, tree branches and planks were placed on them and they were set alight. When police attempted to extinguish the fire bricks and stones were aimed at them. According to SAPS, when police officers arrived the community opened fire on them. Police called in the Public Order Policing Unit who dispersed the crowd with no injuries. It wan’t the first time residents in the area had attacked police officers. In January 2019 it was reported that about 200 residents had turned on officers conducting a drug raid in Shallcross, in the same street where Teddy lived. Teddy Mafia succumbed to his injuries in a Chatsworth hospital. THE LOVE / HATE RELATIONSHIP Pillay was loved and despised by the Chatsworth community. The Shallcross community, which benefited from his charity including food parcels. Word in the community is that he put kids through school and university and even helped people pay their utility bills. It’s said that if you were in trouble you could turn to Teddy who would help where he could. Alleged criminal syndicates and leaders are often viewed as Robin Hood-type characters as the proceeds of crime often go back into the community, so if a drug lord is killed, it would directly affect the community. It’s a tactic utilised by criminal syndicates around the world who purposely and strategically look after their community so they are given cover and protection when the time comes. The reality is whether it is an act of vigilantism because of mistrust in police, a message by associates of Teddy Mafia or the community seeking revenge because of who was killed, there was a total sense of impunity and disregard for the law. At least two people a day die as a result of vigilante or group attacks in South Africa, according to the Institute for Security Studies. Violence is so normalised in society that ‘ordinary’ people commit horrific acts. UNSOLVED DRIVEBY SHOOTINGS THE START OF VIOLENT CLASHES And in March 2020 Pillay’s son Devendren was fatally wounded in a drive-by shooting in Shallcross (Chatsworth). It is understood that Devendren Lionel Pillay, 32, and Claudene Rampersad, 32, had been standing in the driveway of Rampersad’s home on Alpine Drive, Shallcross, when a white Toyota Corolla, with a number of occupants, drove past and fired multiple shots — killing the pair. Around the same time there were at three other relatives of Teddy taken out, and what was believed to be retaliation shooting killing some of his rival gang members. TEDDY’s BRUSHES WITH THE LAW Despite Teddy Mafia’s reign spanning more than three decades – he was never convicted of drug offences. He has been arrested a few times – the most recent was arrested in April 2020 during a raid at his home, where police allegedly found unlicensed firearms, R700,000 in cash, and gold and silver coins with an estimated value of R250,000. Charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition, he was released on R5,000 bail at the Chatsworth magistrate’s court and ordered to appear at the local police station twice a week. Previous convictions dating back to the 1970s for dealing in alcohol, driving without a licence and possession of an unlicensed firearm. But no drug convictions. TEDDY’s BROTHER SPEAKS OUT Ronnie Pillay, lambasted the police, saying there was a drug war taking place in Shallcross and police had done nothing to make any arrests in relation to the eight murders which had occurred since December 2019. “There is corruption with police and criminals. The police are well aware of what is transpiring in this country — they are well aware. There is a drug war taking place here, there's a drug war in regard to sales and distribution.” He went on to claim there were links between certain “drug lords” in Durban and senior police officials, claiming the rot stretched as far as senior officials in Pretoria WHAT WE HAVE - Videos from the scene – the beheadings, the burning of the bodies - Voice Notes from the police on the scene calling for back up. - Teddy Mafia’s brother on camera. INTERVIEWS - SAPS - RONNIE PILLAY – BROTHER: CRITICISED SAPS FOR SITUATION IN COMMUNITY – DOESN’T DENY BROTHER’S ILLEGAL ACTIVITIES – SAYS HE WAS WHO HE WAS. - ORRIN SINGH – JOURNALIST: ABOUT THE BACKGROUND AND HOW EVENTS UNFOLDED ON THE DAY - ANDREW FAULL – ISS: THE SAVAGE COMBINATION OF GANGSTERISM AND MOB JUSTICE. - COP INSIDER – STILL WORKING ON IT – WITHIN SAPS COPS FEEL THEY ARE TO BLAME – THE ORGANISED CRIME INVESTIGATIONS ARE INEFFECTIVE BECAUSE COPS ARE ON THE TAKE AND DESPITE BEING LAW ENFORCERS THEY FEAR THE GANGS.
